newsitem.title: USA: Construction spending rebounds in August.
newsitem.headline: Construction spending rebounds in August.

text.p: New construction spending rebounded in August from a July drop, the Commerce Department said Wednesday, as private builders picked up the slack from a slumping pubic sector.

Total spending on new projects rose 0.9 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $562.1 billion in August, recovering most of a revised 1.1 percent decline in July. Previously, the department said July spending was down more sharply, by 1.4 percent.
All the increase in August spending occurred in the private sector, where outlays increased 1.3 percent to a rate of $423.4 billion following a 1.2 percent decline in July.
By contrast, public, or taxpayer-financed, building projects posted a third straight monthly drop, falling 0.2 percent after declines of 0.7 percent in July and 0.3 percent in June.

Analysts said the pickup in August building was not robust enough to alter the picture of a slowing economy in the final six months of this year. Most expect second-half growth to ease to an annual rate around 2.5 percent from the second quarter's 4.7 percent surge, when national output was rising at the fastest clip in two years.

"Despite the 0.9 percent increase in construction spending during August, these data fit well with the view that the economy slowed significantly in the third quarter of the year," said economist Marilyn Schaja of Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp. in New York.

Averaging July and August figures, Schaja said construction spending was down significantly from the second-quarter pace. The third quarter ended on Sept. 30, so there is one more month of data yet to come on construction.

During August, private-sector spending on non-residential building construction climbed strongly, by 3 percent, to a record rate of $139.5 billion after a 1.6 percent drop in July. Spending increased to build new hotels, schools, hospitals and commercial buildings.
Spending on residential buldings -- single-family homes and apartments -- was flat at a $244-billion annual rate in August after falling 1.1 percent in July.

On the public construction side, there was notably reduced spending in August for new highways and streets and smaller declines for conservation and military projects. More was spent on sewers, schools and water supply plants.

Economist Cynthia Latta of DRI/McGraw Hill Inc. in Lexington, Mass., speculated that after a severe winter, many municipalities may have been forced to trim budgets for road repair because they spent so much earlier.

Even so, she said, "Construction is going to remain a small positive for overall economic growth" for the rest of the year. Private builders are active and there are signs the office market, which was moribund for months because of a glut of available space, is starting to recover with more building of retail stores.
"We will see some growth in the non-residential private sector and pretty steady spending on residential construction," Latta said.
After allowing for inflation, total construction spending was up 0.7 percent in August to a seasonally adjusted $488.1-billion annual rate after a 1.6 percent fall in July, the department said.
